Params: On the ship's deck, the cold drove the rescued survivors to huddle together, trying to wipe away the saltwater and the fear still clinging to their skin.

Pyroclastic debris from an undersea eruption had surged to the surface, and waves towering over ten meters had flipped their vessels in moments. The base's rescue ship had only managed to pull a handful of survivors from the water.
Most are holding up okay. Some injuries. Probably hit by falling debris when the ships went over. Getting a full count will take a while.
The distress calls keep coming... Are we really the only rescue team out here? Where's the air support? What the hell is everyone else doing...
Onni kept his voice low, his eyes traveling past the gunwale to the gray, shrouded horizon.
The sea was not always merciful. Humanity hungered for her strength, so they shaped the current projects into reins, hoping to tame her fury as one might break a wild horse.
From children learning the rules, to sages who mastered them, and at last to new gods who rewrote them altogether.
Where's Alec? He was right behind us.
He scanned the huddled survivors, looking for the face he knew.

They were from the Fortuna, and they had been fortunate. A disrupted current had driven a mass of superheated water into the regular sea, swelling the hull until the welded seams split and seawater poured in. The breach was caught early. Almost no one was lost.
But among the saved, his friend was not there.
Last I saw him, he said he was going back for his toolbox... Should've been fast. Bop-A152 already got it up to the deck...
...I can't find him anywhere. He didn't make it out?!
They exchanged a glance, then said nothing more.
Given how fast the hull had been flooding, the Fortuna had likely gone under already.
Soon, the naval vessel's personnel began counting heads and cataloging injuries. Alec's name was added to the missing list.
That was all. No one, not even his friends, was foolish enough to ask to turn back.

A mass of dark clouds churned across the distant sea line, fast approaching. The sight spoke of a storm, but Gunnar's instincts told him otherwise. He believed it was a warning passed down through his bloodline.
Alright, we're loaded. Let's go back!
The sea was speaking a warning, and Gunnar, a man shaped by a lifetime on the water, knew better than to ignore it.
A blast of the ship's whistle flung a seabird skyward, the wind catching beneath its wings and bearing it toward a far-off horizon.
The bird crossed above the half-sunken deck of the Fortuna. Down below, a Bop-A152 unit raised its gaze to follow the sound.

Blood pattered down its metal arm. Sprawled on the deck was a young man in maintenance coveralls, his open tool kit beside him. Its contents littered the deck, a scattered echo of the wound torn through his belly.
Across the distant continent, celebratory salvoes shattered into wails of agony. The calamity called the Punishing Virus extended its brutal greetings to the arrogant human world.
The new gods, who had reached into forbidden places, were granted an invitation to the Filtering. On the winds, atmospheric rivers brought new arrivals without end to these seas.
Humanity had not yet healed from the wounds of the Atlantic Calamity, and already the shadow of the Punishing Virus was seeping into the pulse of the world.
North Atlantic, Rainbow Bridge Military Base.
Gunnar's unit had left first, and nearly all the remaining detachments were now scattered across the sea on rescue duty. Cordelia found herself working alongside Lumi out of necessity.
Are these all distress calls? I've never seen them this dense before...
On the monitor that marked distress signals, clusters of red dots multiplied with terrifying speed, crawling and pulsing across the entire sea like a malignant rash consuming healthy skin.
This is way past anything the system predicted.

She had sent out transmission after transmission for thirty minutes straight. Every single one went unanswered. It was as if this stretch of ocean had been erased from the map, forsaken by everyone beyond it.
Still nothing? I tried reaching our instructors at F.O.S. too... I can't even get a link established.
Lumi's eyes moved across the distress signals as they winked out one by one, like dying flaps of skin sloughing away.
Her lips were clamped tight. Cordelia gave her a light pat on the head and pressed a fingertip to her knitted forehead until the tension eased.
What's with the little old lady face? First apocalypse? Relax. You get the hang of it after a few.
A few... What do you mean, a few?
Lumi stared at Cordelia's beaming face for a few long seconds before it dawned on her that she was being teased.
You can still crack jokes at a time like this, Ms. Erhorn.
You looked about two seconds away from passing out. Had to do something.
Hey, Lumi. Your theory grades are pretty solid, right? Help me out with something.
I need you to filter out the automated alerts, standard format stuff, and pull anything that was manually entered.
Then extract the keywords and analyze the information. Let's try to figure out what's actually happening out there.
Or are you planning to just sit here and wait for some commander or instructor to tell you what to do?
Cordelia patted Lumi on the shoulder again and gave her a playful wink.
Look, Lumi, if this is an apocalypse movie, you don't get to sit around waiting for someone to hand you the script.
Here, take a look at this.
The virtual panel she called up wavered badly, its display stuttering between light and dark.
What... what am I looking at?
Status map. Every hub node in the Transatlantic fiber-optic comm network.
Normally, it'd be a clean blue and green web. Instead, we've got... whatever the hell this is. Looks like a brain about to blow a fuse...
Lumi stared, transfixed, at the gray-white blotches peeling across the display like shed snakeskin.
But this system... isn't it classified?
Huh? That's your takeaway? Fine, fine... I'm from the awful Erhorn family. I'm one of the damn elites. I don't care about clearance levels, and my access is high enough to get me wherever I want.
That fits your spoiled heiress stereotype nicely?
Cordelia pulled a silly face at the young girl.
Relax. This kind of system is read-only for me. No touching.
See this? It's the first node that went offline. The last log entry is a perfectly clean self-diagnostic. No error codes. No system alerts. It just...
Seventeen minutes before it dropped, a clear command appeared in the offline log. The node executed a manual shutdown. Only a node's direct supervisor has that kind of clearance.
And this isn't just one node. Almost every offline node follows one of two scripts. Either it dies without any warning at all... or it kills itself, fast and deliberate.
Node shutdown requires the highest clearance level of any operation. This speed and this scope we're seeing right now... It shouldn't be possible theoretically.
And if a real disaster hit... the nodes should be opening up and screaming for backup, not going dark.
So what we're looking at... it might not be human action at all but some kind of natural disaster...?
I haven't figured that part out yet... Could be something hijacking their clearances... Cyber warfare, something like that.
Whatever's happening, I doubt the mainland's faring much better. Probably why we can't get a comm link established.
So... you want to figure out what caused all of this?
A dam explosion and the current projects going offline... that doesn't explain any of this, of course.
Cordelia's eyes lingered on the holographic node map, its lines shriveling like desiccated creepers.
A seabird landed on the sill, shrieking. Lumi's attention slipped from her logging for a heartbeat; the bird's tail was soaked in red.
It had flown far. All it needed now was a brief perch, a moment to comb the blood from its feathers.
No visible injuries. So where did the blood...?
Hundreds of miles away, what was left of the blood's source—half a torso and little more—rocked in the pale spume behind a cargo ship.
The vessel was the Golden Apple, sailing from the Arctic Route Union, now creeping at three knots through a scattered cortege of limbs.
Creatures that had once been men had been gutted by the propeller, their remains wrapped around the shaft, wafting underwater.
A Corrupted, one of the deranged machines soon to be named so by a terrified humanity, leaned over the side and scanned the waves.
It was hunting the human who had leaped for life. Below, a pale spine poked through dark red tissue like a broken length of cable core.

The spray of blood from his severed body had shot high and struck a passing bird. All that remained of him beyond that floating wreckage were those few crimson stains, borne aloft and carried far from the nightmare below.
Then the bird landed on a sill at Rainbow Bridge Base.
Cordelia fixed her eyes on the seabird's blood-stained feathers, her expression unreadable.
Cordelia could not know whether White Stork remained trapped upon the ocean or had already slipped away to a distant, unbound shore.
Another piercing cry rang out as someone leaped into the sea.
Inside the stairwell, screams and alarms wove together in a rolling tide, and every gasp of air felt viscous, as if the atmosphere had turned to sludge.

The cold storage door, designed to keep everything out, swallowed most of the commotion. But the high, piercing screams still forced their way through the reinforced metal, reaching White Stork's ears.
She was hiding in the deck galley's produce room. Near the door lay the frozen fish the head chef had meant for the evening banquet, and the head chef himself, silent forever.
The sound of machinery splitting a frozen fish was not so different from the sound it made splitting a person.
The blade bit in and spun at high speed. Over the steady, orderly hum, everything inside the belly was reduced to slurry. Perhaps that was the only difference.
Outside, the screams of her own kind erupted once more. Humans begged, shrieked, and fought for their last ragged breaths.
The same shrill, grinding noise accompanied them, so close it might as well have been inside her own skull. White Stork shuddered involuntarily, her arms tightening around the baby in her grip.
She knew that sound. Before the cold storage door had sealed her off from the world outside, she had watched a passenger get carved in two at the waist.
(Model Bop-A152. Rotation speed 47000 RPM... They'll need to recharge soon...)
(If I can just hold out till then... I can make a run for the captain's cabin and get a distress call out... Just a little longer...)

The Bop-A152 had been a capable all-purpose support machine before the Mannan line took over. Right up until three hours ago, when it decapitated its first human, it had remained the most beloved service robot available.
It was agile and brightly colored, with a default voice that piped up like an eager child. Told to laugh, it would throw its arms up and whirl around in joyful circles.
In the words of the barmaid from the deck bar, it looked like a crazy clown.
Now it really went crazy. Every intelligent machine onboard had snapped. People fled and clawed past one another, only to be caught and reduced to torn flesh swaying from mechanical grips.
White Stork had forced her way into the produce room and added her biometrics to the lock.
The room, keyed now to biological signals alone, served as a makeshift refuge.
The shriek of spinning blades continued without pause. White Stork hunched her shoulders, her arms wrapped entirely around the baby. There was no hand left to shield her own ears.
(Go away... get away from here... get away from me...)

White Stork caught a glimpse of the baby's eyes. She was holding her so tight she could hardly breathe herself, her arms clenched around the tiny body. The moment she realized, she forced herself to ease her grip.
The strange child showed no reaction at all.
Still, White Stork treated her like any ordinary child, rocking her gently and pressing a careful fingertip to the baby's lips.

The vivid colors of the produce around her glinted in her lifeless eyes. Beyond the cold storage door, the shrieks of fellow humans sounded in broken intervals. The creatures of civilization were being culled inside a steel ocean jungle, butchered by the very civilization they had built.
The baby girl only looked at White Stork, expressionless, motionless, silent as a porcelain shrine figure with blank, staring eyes.
A vessel for a god, stolen by her.
Perhaps White Stork herself had gone crazy as well.
Then the baby's pupils gave the faintest tremor. Outside the door, the hurried footsteps multiplied, drawing closer and closer.
The produce room door was yanked open. It was the barmaid from the deck bar, and White Stork only had time to catch the wild terror in her eyes.
She instinctively clutched the baby tighter, using her arm to cover the child's face.
****! ...Don't just stand there blocking the way! Move! MOVE!!!
You piece of ****! You trying to get us all killed?!
In that fleeting glance, the barmaid understood at once that the tiny room could not hold more than one.
Without a second thought, she moved to close the door.
A steel bar smashed into her skull in the next second. She dropped, and behind her stood a man with murder in his eyes, flanked by a few other survivors.
Hogging it for yourself? Screw you!
The crazy clowns she used to mock did not end her life. A fellow human brought her down with a steel bar, just outside the door of a refuge.
The man with the steel bar ignored her completely. He stepped over the barmaid's fallen body and stretched his hand toward White Stork, ready to haul her out.
Get out! I'm taking that spot!
Not everyone understood what had just happened. But once the first hand shot forward, a second followed, and then a third.
The survivors surged toward the doorway, every single arm stretching out in desperation.
Each hand moved with the crowd, driven by nothing but the raw instinct to live.
Blast after blast tore through the sea's surface, piling fresh, senseless agony onto the nightmare already unfolding.
The scent of the sea had shifted, just slightly. Beneath the familiar salt and brine, the wind now carried something sharp and invasive.
Onni sniffed at the air, a vague restlessness prickling under his skin.

Lieutenant Onni, the last group of survivors is settled in Cabin 3. Injury reports are sent back to base. Lumi says we're short on medical supplies. She wants us to keep an eye out during the next sweep.
Onni glanced at the young cadet and gave his cigarette case a few quiet taps.
Mm... Stay sharp today. You got me?
Huh? Oh, yeah, yeah. Got it, Captain!
Tch... Silly kid. And it's not just meds. Grab food too. Whatever you can find.
Onni's unease was soon vindicated. The second time he pulled out his cigarette case, the first mate's voice burst through the communicator.
Commander Gunnar. Cargo vessel on approach, bearing steady. No course change in accordance with COLREG. Call sign APL-307. No response to hails. Attempting sixth contact now.
Keep hailing. Onni? Onni! Cigarette later. Get back here. We're turning.
Onni tucked the unlit cigarette back into its case with a rueful grimace.
...What's their problem? Doesn't look like they're here to make friends.
Check her course history. Any route deviations on record?
She's still accelerating... At this speed, she'll hit us. We're running out of time to turn.
Gunnar's brow creased. The scent of the sea had turned dangerous. The air, always so sharp and clean before, now carried a faint, creeping hint of rust.
On the chart, the ship was still gaining speed, cutting a near-perfect line straight toward the Karenin.
Onni worked the helm, and the ship leaned hard to one side.
She's almost inside the perimeter. Fire a warning shot!
A volley of small missiles shot from the Karenin, skimming low over the clear water before erupting across the surface.
The oncoming vessel, still gaining speed, swerved to evade them anyway, but those missiles were never meant to strike true.
Sir! They're evading even the warning shots...
An explosion ripped through the air and echoed across the bridge.
Amid the chaos, the comms hissed with static, a call coming through from base.
There's a cargo ship heading straight for you... Sink it!
I'm requesting emergency authorization to engage!
Karenin, this is Rainbow Bridge Military Base. Target call sign APL-307. Sink it immediately. I repeat, sink it immediately.
With a deep hydraulic groan, the primary gun turret swung around.
It shifted in minute increments, steadying itself, then fixed squarely on the cargo ship.
The barrel's dark opening stared without emotion.
The dark hollow of the muzzle stared back, the spiral of its rifling just visible in the depths.
Superheated gas and flecks of unburnt powder vented from the sides of the barrel.
The infant girl's pupils shuddered violently, and she lifted her chin a fraction. It was the biggest movement she had ever made in White Stork's arms.
The bullet punched clean through the man's lower leg. He stumbled forward and crashed down, both knees slamming into the deck.
This was the man who had first attacked outside the produce room.
The woman who had fired the shot was gulping for breath, blood trickling from the wound in her scalp and threading through her disheveled hair.
In the face of the malice born of desperate survival, there was nothing else she could do.
Only moments earlier, before the shots and explosions had erupted, the crowd had surged into the produce room.
Fingers tangled in White Stork's hair and yanked at her clothes, dragging her body halfway out.
Protecting the baby meant she could not fight back, and the predators saw it. Their hands moved toward the baby.
<color=#ffffffff><size=60>Not the child. Anyone but the child.</size></color>
A massive detonation ripped across the water. It was from the Karenin's gun batteries, speaking on Gunnar's order.

Clouds of smoke and concussion waves rolled over the surface. Far off, the Golden Apple burned where the missile had found her, and all eyes turned toward the dying ship as she slid beneath the flames.
At that same moment, White Stork's bullet found its mark: the man who had been the first to attack.
Get away! Get AWAY! GET AWAY—
None of them knew why the Golden Apple had suddenly been struck down, just as none had expected a weapon in the young woman's hands.
The last reverberations of the shot and the blasts had died away. The barmaid lay crumpled in the doorway, a dark pool of blood creeping outward beneath her.

The quiet was suffocating. White Stork's grip on the gun quivered, but every hand that had tried to haul her out now withdrew and disappeared into the crowd, like a stain vanishing into the ocean. All the ugliness and malice vanished right along with them.
Each hand had belonged to someone ready to survive at another's expense, and none of them thought themselves guilty.

They were also the woman who had laid a coat over her shoulders, the young man who had pointed her in the right direction, and the woman who had told her what temperature the baby's formula should be...
Desperation and disaster had crushed something fragile and precious in them all.
All of you... get away from me!!
Those quiet, weightless sorrows she had carried spilled over, turning into tears escaping before she could stop them.
She lowered her face, let the cloth of the baby's blanket catch the moisture, and pulled herself back into the shelter of the produce room.
30 Minutes Ago, Rainbow Bridge Military Base, North Atlantic.

"The control systems are going down level by level. We tried shutting them off from the top, but Petrolina's faster... She doesn't need any authorization. She's going to kill—AAGH!" ...That was a distress call from an offshore drilling platform.
Petrolina is their central AI. Don't bother writing that name down, Detective Lumi.
Detective? Ms. Erhorn... please be serious.
Serious? Alright. Lumi, how many AIs have we logged so far that are busy slaughtering humans?
Cordelia exhaled a quiet sigh, her face settling into a grim expression.
Lumi ran her eyes over the transmissions, each one classified and recorded by her own hand.
"Don't trust any of them... Bop's gone crazy..." Bop-A152, the most common general-purpose robot on the Atlantic routes.
"Please... the machines have all gone mad... no, don't hurt me... someone help..." A summer camp trip... That ship was full of kids.
Machines, madness... and killing. The pattern's clear. We're in the middle of a machine uprising. Is it some kind of malfunction?
Feeling the weight of the moment, Lumi squeezed her eyes shut in pain.
Keep working, Lumi. We're the ones who have to unravel this "apocalypse."

Cordelia's face remained unchanged, her work proceeding with apparent composure. But between checks of the data, her fingers tapped an unconscious rhythm against the tabletop, betraying her true state.
She had grown too used to hiding behind jokes, yet humor born of fear did nothing to quiet the fear itself.
She shook her head, tilted her face toward the ceiling, and felt her heart slowly swallowed by dread.
From everything we have, this looks more like a virus. One that targets intelligent machines. A plague that could bring down an entire industrial civilization.
Contact APL-307. Bearing one-zero-seven. Speed thirty-five knots, closing. Issue warning?
A sudden blare from the radar alarm jolted Cordelia from her thoughts.
On the Karenin. This is the base escort radar. It's tracking the Karenin.
Cordelia strode quickly to the main radar console. A single blip had surfaced on the horizon, closing at a speed no cargo ship could match.
It ignored every hail from the base and broadcast no identification code, driving toward the Karenin with the single-minded purpose of a torpedo.
A warning? That thing's last registered ID was a cargo ship called Golden Apple. Now it's loaded with guns and outrunning military vessels. You really think a warning's going to do anything?
Its AI's gone mad too. Thinks it's a torpedo now, apparently. Creative. I'll give it that...
Cordelia drew a long, steadying breath.
If we don't, it's going to T-bone the Karenin. And then we'll have two wrecks instead of one.
But I don't have clearance to fire!
The girl practically shrieked the words out.
Contact BAL-001. Bearing three-zero-seven. Speed twenty-five knots. No response. No ID. Approaching base.
The central AI sounded another alarm. This time, a warship was bearing down on them, and the target was the military base where the two of them stood.
Incoming transmission received. Decoding... Playing now.
A blood-streaked face filled the screen.
Rainbow Bridge... this is the cruiser Balder. Sink us immediately...
Balder's AI is compromised. It's attacking everything on the surface. No exceptions.
Our engineer overrode the speed limiter before he died. By our heading... you're the closest guns. You can... sink us before it's too late.
The machines onboard went berserk. Everyone is dead. There's no one left to rescue. Don't wait. Before you're inside the Balder's firing envelope... shoot us down.
I've transmitted the engineer's final logs and data with this message. I hope—AARGH!
A sickening screech of grinding metal rang out, and before the two girls' eyes, a massive mechanical crab claw seized the blood-soaked officer by the waist and lifted him into the air.
The young officer, already broken beyond saving, did not fight it. His hand moved faintly, reaching for a final salute he no longer had the strength to finish.
I salute you... my fellow humans...
The transmission cut out without warning. The blood-smeared face, still caught in a smile, vanished from the screen, frozen over by the monstrous iron claws of a Mannan-4.
Cordelia slammed her palm against the console, biting down on the swear words rising in her throat.
Lumi. Patch me through to the Karenin.
On it. They must already see the Golden Apple acting strange...
But they don't necessarily know how bad strange can get.
The live feed from the Karenin flickered onto the screen.
The infected cargo ship Golden Apple wore no mask over its hostility, and the crew of the Karenin did not waver. Commander Gunnar gave the order to sink her immediately.
Amid the thunder of cannons, the Golden Apple marched into its grave.

Using the live communication channel between the base and the Karenin, Cordelia found her opening the moment the cannons roared. She punched through a vulnerability and hijacked a privileged access account.
To steal a treasure from the grip of a devil, she had to steal the devil's power first.
Across the entire TEC, Arius' authorization granted passage everywhere.
But even a devil's authority could be turned to something better.
Once the special access account was connected, the central AI fell obedient, no longer sounding warnings.
Command: Target bearing three-zero-seven. Warship Balder. You are weapons free.
Wielding the devil's own authority, Cordelia at last fulfilled the dying plea of the officer whose name she would never learn.
I salute you, my fellow human.
Ignoring the launch feed, Cordelia reopened the management interface for the base AI.
Frigga's status still registered as blue-green, but the encroaching gray-white stain had crept to within a sliver of consuming it entirely.
Her mouth set in a thin line. The Balder disappeared from the radar screen, descending into the deep with its final duty done.
Ms. Erhorn, did the base just sink a warship?
I accept full responsibility, Commander Gunnar.
And... there's a final message for you to see, from the Balder. Also... I apologize for overstepping earlier.
Lumi patched the Balder's final transmission through to the Karenin and quietly explained the full sequence of events.
Cordelia slumped back in her seat, exhaling in one deep release, and stared up at the pale, colorless ceiling.
It held nothing visible. Yet she knew the central AI Frigga hung suspended in that emptiness, waiting in silence for her direction.
(A blessing wrapped in disaster? I was reckless enough to steal that baby... Reckless enough to lay my hands on the devil's own scepter.)
Frigga, raise the base's missile defense to maximum.
Frigga would no longer refuse any request she made.
Defense level adjusted. Missile defense system operating at full capacity.
Frigga, switch base operations to manual mode.
Advisor Cordelia, will you no longer require my services?
Frigga, I think... you need a good, long rest.
"A long rest"? Advisor Cordelia, I am unable to determine a specific timeframe from that phrasing.
Cordelia's eyes tracked down the columns of data until they settled on the offline protocol, buried at the bottom of the list.
It's a vacation, you know... and a vacation, ideally, shouldn't have a set end date. The longer, the better, really.
She still couldn't resist cracking jokes with an artificial intelligence.
Frigga, thank you for your service. I'll see you later.
She pressed the red button. The blue lights of Frigga went dark, one after another.
Ms. Erhorn, how bad is it?
Every machine with an intelligent system has been compromised... Accident or conspiracy, it doesn't matter. What we're facing is a virus, one that targets intelligent machines.
A virus... that infects intelligent machines?
Yes. We can't trust... any central AI anymore.
Commander Gunnar, shut down all intelligent systems and every smart device on board. Then head back as fast as you can.
Don't approach any vessel that doesn't respond. And for your own protection, I recommend heavy weapons... And use them first, not last.
Are you insane? There are civilians out there.
They're more likely the enemy by now.
In this ocean-borne apocalypse, the Balder became the first warship to go down.
The sea boiled and heaved for endless days and nights after, the moon watching over tide after tide, until the Balder finally sailed upon these waters again.
Deep into the night, rows of protocol code flow like water across the virtual screen. When Lucia steps through the door, Lee is buried deep in that sea of data.
Commandant and I calculated the timing and routes. For the Balder to reach the Atlantic Eye on time, we have to split up in three directions.
A slight movement of Lucia's fingers, and the holographic data weaves itself into a nautical chart.
The Balder holds course for the Atlantic Eye. She'll handle the repeater replacements at Jormungandr, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge node, along the way.
We two take the modified repeaters and the new protocol overland. Full speed to Hel, the northern node. If we find a station, we contact the Arctic Route Union for support.
Commandant and Karenina take the cable layer south to Fenrir. Figure out what happened there, swap everything out, then loop back and finish the Jormungandr line.
How long do I have to finish the provisional protocol?
Lee stays hunched at the controls, his hands moving in a continuous, rapid rhythm.
Teddy and I have very different coding styles. Building on top of her work means I have to be extra thorough. So...
Half an hour should do it.
The joke draws a faint smile from both of them.
Code streams down the display like a waterfall. The hardest problem is clearly solved, and only the finishing touches remain.
Looks like you won't need the full thirty.
Then I'll get started on our departure prep for the northern node, Hel.
Lucia steps out of the cabin and lifts her eyes to the bright moon overhead.
(...Liv's probably asleep by now. I hope the dreams are good to her tonight...)
